Computer hardware and software

Computer Hardware Basics

Hardware – any physical device or equipment used in or with a computer system (anything you can see and touch).

Hardware is divided into 2 major categories: External and Internal. Without hardware, software cannot run. Example: Even if you have Windows, if you have no monitor, CPU, or keyboard, you cannot use it. Hardware works together like a human body – CPU is the brain, RAM is short-term memory, Hard Drive is long-term memory.

WHAT IS A COMPUTER SYSTEM?

A computer system = Hardware + Software + Peopleware + Data.

Hardware: Physical parts

Software: Programs

Peopleware: User / IT / Programmer

Data: Information processed

4 Basic Operations: Input → Process → Output → Storage (IPOS Cycle)

External hardware

External hardware devices (peripherals) – any hardware device that is located outside the computer.

Peripherals are connected via USB, HDMI, Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, VGA. 3 types: Input, Output, Input/Output (Storage). Example of Input/Output device: Touchscreen, USB Flash Drive, External Hard Drive.

Input device – a piece of hardware device which is used to enter information to a computer for processing.

Other Input Devices: Scanner, Barcode Reader, Digital Camera, Graphics Tablet, Biometric Scanner (fingerprint), OMR, OCR, MICR, Sensor. Keyboard types: Mechanical, Membrane, Wireless, Ergonomic. Mouse types: Optical, Laser, Wireless, Trackball.

Input devices in details

Keyboard: 101-104 keys, QWERTY layout, Function keys F1-F12

Mouse: Click, Double-click, Right-click, Scroll, Drag

Microphone: Converts sound to digital signal

Webcam: Captures video for video call / streaming

Joystick: Used for games and simulators / flight control

Touchscreen: Input + Output in one

Examples: keyboard, mouse, trackpad (or touchpad), touchscreen, joystick, microphone, light pen, webcam, speech input, etc.

Output device – a piece of hardware device that receives information from a computer.

Note: Scanner is actually Input Device, not Output – common exam trap. Output is divided into Soft Copy (Monitor, Speaker) and Hard Copy (Printer). Speaker produces sound output, Projector produces large visual output.

OUTPUT DEVICES IN DETAIL ]

Monitor: LCD, LED, OLED. Resolution: 720p, 1080p, 4K. Measured in inches and refresh rate Hz.

Printer: Inkjet, Laser, Dot Matrix, Thermal, 3D Printer

Speaker / Headphone: Converts digital audio to sound

Projector: Projects image to wall/screen for classroom/presentation

Examples: monitor, printer, scanner, speaker, display screen (tablet, smartphone …), projector, head phone, etc.

Internal hardware

Internal hardware devices (or internal hardware components) – any piece of hardware device that is located inside the computer.

Examples: CPU, hard disk drive, ROM, RAM, etc.

Internal hardware is inside System Unit / CPU Box. Also includes: Motherboard, Power Supply Unit (PSU), Graphics Card (GPU), Sound Card, Network Card, Cooling Fan, CMOS Battery.

CPU – Central Processing Unit – Brain of computer.

3 Parts: ALU (Arithmetic Logic Unit), CU (Control Unit), Registers (Memory)

Speed measured in GHz (Gigahertz). Example: 3.5 GHz

Brands: Intel Core i3/i5/i7/i9, AMD Ryzen 3/5/7/9, Apple M1/M2/M3

Functions: Fetch, Decode, Execute, Store

MEMORY: RAM vs ROM

RAM – Random Access Memory: Temporary, volatile. When you turn off PC, data is gone. More RAM = faster multitasking. Types: DDR3, DDR4, DDR5.

ROM – Read Only Memory: Permanent, non-volatile. Contains BIOS. Cannot be easily changed.

Cache Memory: Very fast small memory inside CPU.

STORAGE DEVICES

HDD – Hard Disk Drive: Magnetic, cheaper, larger capacity (500GB-2TB), slower

SSD – Solid State Drive: Faster, no moving parts, more expensive, 256GB-1TB

USB Flash Drive: Portable, 16GB-256GB

CD / DVD / Blu-ray: Optical storage

Cloud Storage: Google Drive, OneDrive, iCloud

MOTHERBOARD AND PSU

Motherboard: Main circuit board. All parts connect here. Has slots for RAM, CPU socket, USB ports.

PSU – Power Supply Unit: Converts AC to DC power for computer.

GPU – Graphics Card: For gaming, video editing, rendering. Example: NVIDIA, AMD Radeon

Cooling System: Fan, Heat Sink, Liquid Cooling – prevents overheating

PORTS AND CONNECTIVITY

USB: For mouse, keyboard, flash drive

HDMI: For monitor / projector / TV

VGA: Old monitor port

Ethernet / LAN: Wired internet

Audio Jack: Speaker / Mic

Bluetooth / Wi-Fi: Wireless connection

Computer Software Basics

Computer software

Software – a set of instructions or programs that tells a computer what to do or how to perform a specific task (computer software runs on hardware).

Main types of software – systems software and application software.

Software is intangible – you cannot touch it. Example: You can touch keyboard (hardware) but you cannot touch Microsoft Word (software). Software needs hardware to run, hardware needs software to be useful.

Application software

Application software – a computer program that provides users with tools to accomplish a specific task.

Examples of application software: word processing, spreadsheets, presentation, database management, Internet browsers, email programs, media players, accounting, pronunciation, translation, desktop publishing, enterprise, etc.

Application Software is also called "Apps" or "End-user programs". It is made for a specific job, not for running the computer itself.

APPLICATION SOFTWARE EXAMPLES IN DETAIL

Word Processing: MS Word, Google Docs, WPS

Spreadsheet: MS Excel, Google Sheets – for computation, tables, graphs

Presentation: MS PowerPoint, Canva, Google Slides

Database: MS Access, MySQL

Browser: Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Safari

Email: Gmail, Outlook, Yahoo Mail

Media Player: VLC, Spotify, YouTube

Graphics: Photoshop, Canva, Figma

System Software

System software – it is designed to run a computer’s hardware and application software, and make the computer system available for use. It serves as the interface between hardware, application software, and the user.

Main functions of system software – allocating system resources, managing storage space, storing and retrieval of files, providing security, etc.

Main types of systems software – operating system, device driver, utility software, programming software, etc.

Without System Software, you cannot open Application Software. Think of it as: System Software = Manager, Application Software = Worker.

Operating system (OS) – a software that controls and coordinates the computer hardware devices and runs other software and applications on a computer. It is the main part of system software and a computer will not function without it.

Main functions of an operating system – booting the computer, managing system resources (CPU, memory, storage devices, printer, etc.), managing files, handling input and output, executing and providing services for application software, etc.

Examples of operating system: Microsoft Windows, Apple iOS, Android OS, macOS, Linux, etc.

Booting = Starting up process. OS loads from Hard Disk to RAM. Types of OS: Single-user (Windows), Multi-user (Linux Server), Real-time (ATM, Robot).

OS COMPARISON

Windows: Most common for PC, made by Microsoft. Windows 10, 11

macOS: For Apple MacBook / iMac only

Linux: Free, open-source, used by programmers

Android: For phones/tablets, made by Google

iOS: For iPhone / iPad, made by Apple

Device driver – a software program that is designed to control a particular hardware device that is attached to a computer.

The main purpose of device driver – it acts as a translator between the hardware device and operating systems or applications that use it.

It instructs computer on how to communicate with the device by translating the operating system’s instructions into a language that a device can understand in order to perform the necessary task.

Examples of device driver: printer driver, display driver, USB driver, sound card driver, motherboard driver, ROM driver, etc.

Example: If you plug a new printer but no printer driver, computer will say "Device not recognized". You need to install driver from CD or download online.

Utility software – a type of system software that helps set up, analyze, configure, strengthen, maintain a computer and performs a very specific task (e.g. antivirus software, backup software, memory tester, screen saver, etc.).

Other Utility Software: Disk Cleanup, Disk Defragmenter, File Compression (WinRAR, ZIP), Firewall, Backup & Restore, Task Manager, System Restore.

PROGRAMMING SOFTWARE

Part of System Software – used to create other software.

Programming Languages: Python, Java, C++, HTML, JavaScript

Tools: Compiler, Interpreter, Debugger, Code Editor (VS Code)

Example: VS Code is used to write programs.

MALWARE AND SECURITY

Virus: Attaches to files, spreads

Worm: Spreads by itself via network

Trojan: Pretends to be useful but harmful

Spyware: Steals information

Protection: Antivirus, Firewall, Update OS, Don't click unknown links

FILE MANAGEMENT

File: Document, Picture, Video, Music

Folder: Container for files

Extensions: .docx (Word), .xlsx (Excel), .pptx (PowerPoint), .pdf, .jpg, .mp3, .mp4

Storage Units: Bit < Byte < KB < MB < GB < TB

1 Byte = 8 Bits, 1 KB = 1024 Bytes

COMPUTER CARE TIPS

Always shut down properly, don't force off

Use antivirus and update regularly

Don't overload storage

Clean keyboard and screen

Keep away from water and heat

Backup important files

1. Understanding How Hardware and Software Work Together

A computer system requires both hardware and software to function properly. Hardware provides the physical equipment, while software provides the instructions that control how the equipment operates.

Hardware and software depend on each other. Hardware cannot perform useful tasks without software, while software cannot operate without compatible hardware.

For example, when a user opens Microsoft Word, the computer uses its processor to execute the program, RAM to temporarily store active information, and the monitor to display the document.

How Hardware and Software Interact

The interaction between hardware and software happens through several processes:

1. User Input

The user provides information using an input device such as a keyboard, mouse, microphone, or touchscreen.

2. Software Instructions

The operating system and application software interpret the user's commands and provide instructions to the computer.

3. Hardware Processing

The CPU processes the instructions and works with other hardware components to complete the requested task.

4. Information Display

The computer sends the processed information to an output device, such as a monitor or printer.

5. Data Storage

If the user saves the information, the computer stores it on a storage device.

Example: Creating a Document

When a student creates an assignment using Microsoft Word:

Keyboard: Used to type the assignment.

Mouse: Used to select commands and options.

Microsoft Word: Provides the tools for creating and editing documents.

Operating System: Manages the computer and allows Word to operate.

CPU: Processes the instructions.

RAM: Temporarily holds the active document and program data.

SSD or HDD: Stores the saved document.

Monitor: Displays the document.

This example demonstrates that hardware and software work together to complete a single computer task.

2. Classification of Computer Hardware According to Function

Computer hardware can be classified according to the functions it performs. Each category has a specific responsibility in the operation of a computer system.

A. Input Hardware

Input hardware refers to devices used to enter data and instructions into a computer.

These devices allow users to communicate with the computer by providing information for processing.

Examples:

Keyboard: Allows users to enter letters, numbers, and commands.

Mouse: Allows users to control the pointer and select objects on the screen.

Scanner: Converts printed documents and images into digital information.

Microphone: Captures sound and sends it to the computer.

Webcam: Captures images and videos.

Barcode Reader: Reads printed barcodes and converts them into digital information.

Biometric Scanner: Captures biological characteristics, such as fingerprints, for identification.

B. Processing Hardware

Processing hardware refers to the components responsible for carrying out instructions and manipulating data.

Examples:

Central Processing Unit (CPU): Executes instructions and performs general processing operations.

Graphics Processing Unit (GPU): Handles graphics-related calculations and parallel processing tasks.

Motherboard: Connects different hardware components and allows them to communicate.

Processing hardware is important because it determines how efficiently a computer performs different tasks.

C. Output Hardware

Output hardware refers to devices that present processed information to users.

Examples:

Monitor: Displays text, images, and videos.

Printer: Produces physical copies of documents and images.

Speaker: Produces audio output.

Headphones: Allow users to listen to sound privately.

Projector: Displays computer output on a larger surface.

D. Storage Hardware

Storage hardware refers to devices that save digital information for temporary or long-term use.

Examples:

Hard Disk Drive (HDD)

Solid-State Drive (SSD)

USB flash drive

Memory card

Optical disc

External storage drive

Storage devices allow users to save documents, applications, photographs, videos, and other digital files.

E. Communication Hardware

Communication hardware allows computers to connect with other devices and exchange information through wired or wireless networks.

Examples:

Network Interface Card (NIC): Allows a computer to connect to a network.

Wi-Fi Adapter: Allows wireless network connections.

Modem: Connects a network to an internet service provider through an appropriate communication technology.

Router: Directs network traffic between connected devices and other networks.

Switch: Connects multiple devices within a local area network.

These devices make communication and information sharing possible.

3. Advanced Input Devices and Their Applications

Input devices have developed beyond traditional keyboards and mice. Modern computers use different technologies to collect information from users and the surrounding environment.

A. Optical Character Recognition (OCR)

OCR is a technology that converts printed or handwritten text in images into machine-readable text.

It is commonly used when converting printed documents into editable digital files.

Applications:

Digitizing books.

Converting scanned documents.

Processing printed forms.

Extracting information from receipts.

B. Optical Mark Recognition (OMR)

OMR is a technology that detects marks made on specially designed forms.

It is commonly used in examinations, surveys, and questionnaires.

For example, an examination sheet with shaded circles can be processed using an OMR scanner to identify selected answers.

C. Magnetic Ink Character Recognition (MICR)

MICR is a technology that reads characters printed using magnetic ink.

It is commonly used in banking, particularly when processing checks.

D. Biometric Input Devices

Biometric devices collect physical or behavioral characteristics to help identify individuals.

Examples:

Fingerprint scanners.

Facial recognition cameras.

Iris scanners.

Voice recognition systems.

These devices are commonly used for device unlocking, attendance systems, and access control.

E. Sensors

Sensors detect physical conditions and convert them into information that a computer can process.

Examples:

Temperature sensors.

Light sensors.

Motion sensors.

Pressure sensors.

Humidity sensors.

Sensors are used in smart homes, industrial equipment, weather monitoring, and healthcare devices.

F. Touch and Gesture Input

Touchscreens allow users to interact directly with displayed objects using their fingers or a compatible stylus.

Gesture recognition systems identify movements and allow users to control devices through specific gestures.

These technologies are commonly found in smartphones, tablets, interactive displays, and modern computer systems.

4. Advanced Output Technologies

Output technologies allow computers to present information in different forms. Modern output devices support higher image quality, improved sound, and more realistic visual experiences.

A. Display Technologies

LCD (Liquid Crystal Display)

LCD monitors use liquid crystals and a backlight to display images. They are commonly used in monitors, televisions, and laptops.

LED (Light-Emitting Diode) Display

Many LED monitors are LCD displays that use LED backlighting. They are known for their energy efficiency and brightness.

OLED (Organic Light-Emitting Diode)

OLED displays use organic materials that produce light individually. They can provide deep blacks, high contrast, and vivid colors.

B. Display Resolution

Resolution refers to the number of pixels used to display an image.

A pixel is the smallest individual element of a digital image.

Common display resolutions include:

720p – 1280 × 720 pixels.

1080p – 1920 × 1080 pixels.

1440p – 2560 × 1440 pixels.

4K UHD – 3840 × 2160 pixels.

Generally, higher resolution provides more image detail when the display and content support it.

C. Refresh Rate

Refresh rate refers to how many times a display updates its image per second.

It is measured in Hertz (Hz).

Examples:

60 Hz.

75 Hz.

120 Hz.

144 Hz.

240 Hz.

Higher refresh rates can provide smoother movement, especially in gaming and animation.

D. Printer Technologies

Inkjet Printer

An inkjet printer produces images and text by spraying small drops of liquid ink onto paper.

It is commonly used for home printing and color photographs.

Laser Printer

A laser printer uses laser technology and toner powder to produce printed documents.

It is commonly used in offices because of its speed and efficiency for large printing tasks.

Dot Matrix Printer

A dot matrix printer uses small pins that strike an ink ribbon to create characters and images.

It is useful in certain environments where multi-copy forms are required.

Thermal Printer

A thermal printer uses heat to produce images or text on specially treated paper or through a thermal transfer process.

It is commonly used for receipts, tickets, and labels.

3D Printer

A 3D printer creates physical objects by building them layer by layer using digital designs.

It is used in engineering, education, product development, and manufacturing.

5. Understanding CPU Performance and Architecture

The Central Processing Unit is one of the most important components of a computer because it executes program instructions.

CPU performance depends on several factors, including clock speed, number of cores, architecture, cache size, and the type of tasks being performed.

A. CPU Clock Speed

Clock speed measures how many cycles a processor performs per second.

It is commonly measured in Gigahertz (GHz).

For example, a processor operating at 3.5 GHz has a clock frequency of approximately 3.5 billion cycles per second.

However, a higher clock speed does not automatically mean that a processor is better. Other factors, such as architecture and core count, also affect performance.

B. CPU Cores

A CPU core is an individual processing unit within a processor.

Modern processors may contain multiple cores that allow them to handle different tasks more efficiently.

Examples:

Dual-core: Two processing cores.

Quad-core: Four processing cores.

Hexa-core: Six processing cores.

Octa-core: Eight processing cores.

A multicore processor can improve performance when applications are designed to use multiple cores.

C. CPU Threads

A thread is a sequence of instructions that can be scheduled for execution by a processor.

Some processors support simultaneous multithreading, which allows a physical core to handle multiple threads.

Threads help improve processor resource utilization and multitasking performance.

D. CPU Cache

Cache memory is a small, high-speed memory located within or close to the processor.

It stores frequently accessed information so that the CPU can retrieve it more quickly.

There are three common levels:

L1 Cache: Very small and extremely fast memory located close to the processing core.

L2 Cache: Usually larger than L1 but generally slower.

L3 Cache: Often shared among multiple CPU cores and usually larger than L1 and L2.

E. The CPU Instruction Cycle

The CPU follows an instruction cycle when executing programs.

1. Fetch

The CPU retrieves an instruction from memory.

2. Decode

The control unit interprets the instruction and determines what action is required.

3. Execute

The CPU performs the requested operation.

4. Store

The result is written to a register or memory location when necessary.

This process repeats continuously while the computer is operating.

6. Understanding Computer Memory and the Memory Hierarchy

Computer memory stores information and instructions needed during computer operations.

Different types of memory have different speeds, capacities, and purposes.

A. Primary Memory

Primary memory is directly accessible by the CPU and is used during normal processing operations.

Examples include RAM and ROM.

Random Access Memory (RAM)

RAM temporarily stores information currently being used by the computer.

It is volatile, which means its contents are normally lost when power is removed.

RAM allows users to run multiple programs and switch between tasks.

Read Only Memory (ROM)

ROM is non-volatile memory used to store important instructions that remain available even when the computer is turned off.

It is commonly associated with firmware and startup-related functions.

B. Secondary Memory

Secondary memory provides long-term storage for files, programs, and other information.

Unlike RAM, it retains stored information when the computer is turned off.

Examples:

HDD.

SSD.

USB flash drive.

Memory card.

Optical disc.

C. Virtual Memory

Virtual memory is a memory management technique used by operating systems.

It allows the system to use part of a storage device as additional memory when physical RAM becomes insufficient.

However, storage devices are generally slower than RAM, so excessive reliance on virtual memory can reduce performance.

D. Memory Hierarchy

Computer memory is arranged according to speed, cost, and storage capacity.

A simplified memory hierarchy is:

CPU Registers – Extremely fast and very small.

Cache Memory – Very fast memory for frequently accessed information.

RAM – Main working memory.

SSD or HDD – Long-term storage.

Generally, faster memory has smaller capacity and higher cost per unit of storage.

Understanding memory hierarchy helps explain why computers use different types of memory instead of relying on only one storage technology.

7. Computer Storage Technologies and File Systems

Storage technology allows computers to preserve information even after the device is turned off.

Different storage devices use different technologies to save and retrieve digital information.

A. Hard Disk Drive (HDD)

An HDD stores information using magnetic surfaces on rotating disks.

It contains mechanical components that move during reading and writing operations.

Advantages:

Usually lower cost per gigabyte.

Available in large storage capacities.

Useful for storing large collections of files.

Disadvantages:

Slower than many SSDs.

Contains moving mechanical parts.

Can be affected by physical shock.

B. Solid-State Drive (SSD)

An SSD stores information using flash memory chips.

It does not use rotating disks or moving read/write heads.

Advantages:

Faster file access.

Faster computer startup.

Quiet operation.

Better resistance to physical movement.

Disadvantages:

Often more expensive per gigabyte than HDDs.

Storage capacity may cost more at the same price level.

C. Optical Storage

Optical storage uses laser technology to read and write information on discs.

Examples:

CD (Compact Disc): Commonly used for music and smaller amounts of digital information.

DVD (Digital Versatile Disc): Offers greater storage capacity than a standard CD.

Blu-ray Disc: Provides greater storage capacity and is commonly used for high-definition video and data storage.

D. Flash Storage

Flash storage uses electronic memory chips to store information.

Examples:

USB flash drives.

SD cards.

microSD cards.

SSDs.

It is widely used because it is compact, portable, and does not require mechanical movement.

E. File Systems

A file system is the method used by an operating system to organize, store, and retrieve information on a storage device.

Common file systems include:

FAT32: An older file system with broad compatibility. It has a maximum individual file size of 4 GB.

exFAT: Designed for flash storage and supports large files. It is commonly used for USB drives and memory cards.

NTFS: Commonly used by Windows systems and supports features such as permissions and large files.

APFS: Apple's file system designed for modern Apple storage devices.

ext4: A commonly used file system in Linux environments.

A file system helps the operating system locate files and manage available storage space.

8. Computer Ports, Cables, and Expansion Slots

Ports and connectors allow hardware devices to communicate with a computer.

They provide connections for displays, storage devices, audio equipment, and network devices.

A. USB Ports

USB stands for Universal Serial Bus.

It is commonly used to connect keyboards, mice, printers, smartphones, and storage devices.

Common USB connector types include:

USB Type-A.

USB Type-B.

USB Type-C.

Micro-USB.

Different USB standards support different data transfer speeds and power capabilities.

B. HDMI

HDMI stands for High-Definition Multimedia Interface.

It transmits digital video and audio signals between compatible devices.

Examples:

Computer to monitor.

Laptop to television.

Computer to projector.

C. DisplayPort

DisplayPort is a digital display interface used to connect computers to monitors.

It supports high-resolution displays and high refresh rates depending on the version and connected equipment.

D. VGA

VGA stands for Video Graphics Array.

It is an older analog video connection commonly found on older computers and monitors.

E. Ethernet Port

An Ethernet port allows computers to connect to wired networks through an Ethernet cable.

It is commonly used for stable local network and internet connections.

F. Audio Ports

Audio ports connect speakers, microphones, and headphones to a computer.

They allow audio signals to enter or leave the system.

G. Expansion Slots

Expansion slots are connectors located on the motherboard that allow additional hardware components to be installed.

Examples:

Graphics cards.

Network cards.

Sound cards.

Storage expansion cards.

PCI Express (PCIe) is a common expansion interface used in modern computers.

9. Understanding Computer Networks and Communication Devices

A computer network is a group of connected computers and devices that communicate and share information.

Networks allow users to share files, printers, applications, and internet connections.

A. Personal Area Network (PAN)

A PAN is a small network that connects devices around one person.

Examples:

Smartphone connected to wireless earbuds.

Laptop connected to a wireless mouse.

Smartphone connected to a smartwatch.

B. Local Area Network (LAN)

A LAN connects computers and devices within a limited geographical area.

Examples:

School computer laboratories.

Office networks.

Home networks.

C. Metropolitan Area Network (MAN)

A MAN connects multiple networks across a city or metropolitan area.

It covers a larger geographical area than a LAN.

D. Wide Area Network (WAN)

A WAN connects computers and networks across large geographical areas, such as different cities or countries.

The internet is the most widely known example of a global network based on interconnected networks.

E. Network Devices

Router

A router directs data between different networks.

Switch

A switch connects multiple devices within a local network and forwards data to the appropriate destination.

Modem

A modem connects a network to an internet service provider through a compatible communication system.

Network Interface Card

A NIC provides a computer with the ability to communicate over a network.

Wireless Access Point

An access point allows wireless devices to connect to a wired network using Wi-Fi.

F. Wired and Wireless Connections

Wired connections use physical cables to transmit data.

Examples:

Ethernet.

Fiber-optic cables.

USB connections.

Wireless connections transmit information without requiring a physical data cable between connected devices.

Examples:

Wi-Fi.

Bluetooth.

Cellular networks.

Both technologies are important in modern computer communication.

10. Understanding Software Licensing and Distribution

Software licensing refers to the legal terms that determine how software can be installed, used, copied, modified, and distributed.

Different software programs have different licensing conditions.

Understanding software licenses helps users avoid copyright violations and unauthorized software use.

A. Proprietary Software

Proprietary software is software owned and controlled by an individual or organization.

Users generally receive permission to use it under specific license conditions.

Examples:

Microsoft Windows.

Microsoft Office.

Adobe Photoshop.

Users may be required to purchase a license or subscription.

B. Open-Source Software

Open-source software makes its source code available under a license that allows certain forms of inspection, modification, and redistribution.

Examples:

Linux.

Mozilla Firefox.

LibreOffice.

GIMP.

Open-source software can be useful for learning programming and understanding how applications work.

C. Freeware

Freeware refers to software that can be used without paying a purchase fee.

However, freeware does not automatically mean that users are allowed to modify or redistribute the software.

Example: Some free desktop applications and utilities.

D. Shareware

Shareware is software distributed for evaluation or limited use.

Users may need to pay for a full version or additional features.

E. Subscription-Based Software

Subscription-based software requires users to pay regularly, such as monthly or annually, to access the service.

Examples include certain versions of Microsoft 365 and Adobe Creative Cloud.

F. Public Domain Software

Public domain software is software that is not restricted by copyright ownership in the usual way.

It may be freely used, modified, and distributed, subject to applicable laws.

Importance of Software Licensing

Software licensing is important because it:

Protects the rights of software developers.

Explains permitted software usage.

Helps prevent unauthorized copying.

Encourages legal software distribution.

Provides users with information about limitations and responsibilities.

11. Programming Languages and Software Development Tools

Programming software allows developers to create applications, websites, operating systems, and other computer programs.

A programming language provides rules and instructions that programmers use to communicate with computers.

A. Machine Language

Machine language is the lowest-level programming language.

It consists of binary instructions represented by 0s and 1s.

It can be directly executed by a processor but is difficult for humans to read and write.

B. Assembly Language

Assembly language uses symbolic instructions that represent machine operations.

It is easier to understand than machine language but still closely connected to the processor's architecture.

An assembler converts assembly language into machine code.

C. High-Level Programming Languages

High-level languages are designed to make programming easier for humans.

Examples:

Python

Python is widely used in automation, data analysis, artificial intelligence, and web development.

Java

Java is used in enterprise applications, software development, and many other computing environments.

C++

C++ is commonly used in system software, games, and performance-intensive applications.

JavaScript

JavaScript is widely used to create interactive websites and web applications.

C#

C# is used in application development, enterprise software, and game development.

D. Programming Language Translators

Compiler

A compiler translates source code into another form, often machine code or executable code, before execution.

Interpreter

An interpreter executes program instructions through an interpreter environment, often processing code as the program runs.

Assembler

An assembler translates assembly language into machine code.

E. Debugging Tools

A debugger is a software tool that helps programmers locate and investigate errors in a program.

It allows developers to examine variables, follow program execution, and identify problems.

F. Code Editors and IDEs

A code editor is a program used to write and edit source code.

An Integrated Development Environment (IDE) combines tools such as code editing, debugging, and building programs.

Examples:

Visual Studio Code.

IntelliJ IDEA.

Eclipse.

Visual Studio.

NetBeans.

These tools help programmers develop and maintain software more efficiently.

12. The Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC)

The Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) is a structured process used to plan, design, develop, test, deploy, and maintain software.

It helps development teams create software that meets user requirements.

Stage 1: Planning

The development team identifies the purpose of the software, its goals, resources, budget, and expected timeline.

Example: A school wants to develop an online student information system.

Stage 2: Requirements Analysis

Developers gather information about what users need from the software.

They identify required features, expected performance, and system limitations.

Example: The school system must allow students to view grades and teachers to manage records.

Stage 3: System Design

Developers plan how the software will work.

This includes designing the user interface, database structure, system architecture, and software components.

Stage 4: Development

Programmers write the source code and create the required features.

They use programming languages, development tools, and frameworks.

Stage 5: Testing

The software is tested to identify errors and determine whether it meets the requirements.

Common types of software testing include:

Unit Testing.

Integration Testing.

System Testing.

Acceptance Testing.

Performance Testing.

Stage 6: Deployment

The completed software is released and made available to users.

It may be installed on computers or hosted through an online service.

Stage 7: Maintenance

Developers continue improving the software after its release.

Maintenance may include fixing errors, improving performance, adding features, and addressing security problems.

Importance of SDLC

The SDLC provides a systematic approach to software development.

It helps teams organize their work, manage resources, identify problems, and produce reliable applications.

13. Computer Viruses, Malware, and Cybersecurity

Computer security is an important part of hardware and software management.

As computers become connected through networks and the internet, they may face different security threats.

Cybersecurity refers to the practices and technologies used to protect systems, networks, and digital information.

A. Types of Malware

Malware means malicious software designed to harm computers, disrupt operations, or gain unauthorized access.

1. Virus

A virus attaches itself to files or programs and may spread when infected files are executed or shared.

2. Worm

A worm can spread across computer networks without needing to attach itself to another program.

3. Trojan Horse

A Trojan disguises itself as legitimate or useful software but performs harmful actions.

4. Spyware

Spyware secretly collects information about a user's activities or device.

5. Ransomware

Ransomware is malware that restricts access to files or systems and demands payment for restoration.

6. Adware

Adware displays unwanted advertisements and may sometimes track user activity.

7. Rootkit

A rootkit is a type of malicious software designed to hide unauthorized activities or maintain privileged access to a system.

B. Security Tools

Antivirus Software

Antivirus software detects, blocks, and removes many types of malicious programs.

Firewall

A firewall monitors network traffic and applies security rules to control incoming and outgoing connections.

Backup Software

Backup software creates copies of important information to help restore files after data loss.

Encryption Software

Encryption software transforms information into a protected format that can only be read using the appropriate decryption method.

C. Safe Computing Practices

Install software from trusted sources.

Keep applications and operating systems updated.

Use strong and unique passwords.

Enable multifactor authentication when available.

Avoid suspicious links and attachments.

Back up important files.

Use secure network connections.

Protect personal and confidential information.

Cybersecurity is not only the responsibility of IT professionals. Every computer user should practice safe and responsible technology use.

14. Common Computer Problems and Basic Troubleshooting

Troubleshooting is the process of identifying, analyzing, and solving problems in a computer system.

Computer problems may be caused by hardware failure, software errors, incorrect settings, insufficient resources, or connectivity issues.

A. Computer Will Not Turn On

Possible causes:

Power cable is disconnected.

Power outlet is not working.

Power supply is faulty.

Battery is empty or damaged.

Basic troubleshooting:

Check the power connection.

Check the power outlet.

Verify that the power switch is turned on.

For laptops, check the charger and battery condition.

Seek technical assistance if the problem continues.

B. Computer Runs Slowly

Possible causes:

Insufficient RAM.

Too many applications running.

Low storage space.

Background processes.

Malware or unwanted software.

Overheating.

Basic troubleshooting:

Close unnecessary applications.

Restart the computer.

Check available storage space.

Review startup applications.

Install available system updates.

Perform a security scan using trusted software.

C. No Display on the Monitor

Possible causes:

Monitor is turned off.

Display cable is disconnected.

Incorrect input source is selected.

Graphics hardware problem.

Basic troubleshooting:

Check the monitor power.

Check the HDMI or DisplayPort connection.

Select the correct input source.

Restart the computer if appropriate.

Request technical assistance if the problem remains.

D. Keyboard or Mouse Is Not Working

Possible causes:

Loose USB connection.

Low wireless battery.

Bluetooth connection problem.

Device driver issue.

Damaged peripheral.

Basic troubleshooting:

Check the device connection.

Try another USB port.

Replace or recharge the battery if necessary.

Check Bluetooth settings.

Restart the device if needed.

E. Computer Has No Internet Connection

Possible causes:

Wi-Fi is disabled.

Router connection is interrupted.

Network cable is disconnected.

Internet service is unavailable.

Incorrect network configuration.

Basic troubleshooting:

Check whether Wi-Fi is enabled.

Verify the router's status.

Check the Ethernet cable if using a wired connection.

Restart network equipment when appropriate.

Contact the internet service provider if the issue continues.

F. Printer Is Not Printing

Possible causes:

Printer is disconnected.

Paper is unavailable.

Ink or toner is empty.

Incorrect printer is selected.

Printer driver has a problem.

Basic troubleshooting:

Check the printer's power.

Check the paper supply.

Check ink or toner levels.

Verify the printer connection.

Review the print queue.

Check the printer driver.

Importance of Troubleshooting

Troubleshooting helps users identify problems before requesting professional repair.

It can reduce downtime, improve productivity, and help prevent unnecessary replacement of computer equipment.

However, users should avoid opening power supplies or performing repairs that require specialized training.

15. Computer Maintenance and Proper Care

Computer maintenance refers to the activities performed to keep computer systems in good working condition.

Regular maintenance improves reliability, protects information, and helps extend the useful life of computer equipment.

A. Preventive Maintenance

Preventive maintenance involves performing regular activities to reduce the possibility of computer problems.

Examples:

Physical Cleaning

Remove dust and dirt from external surfaces using appropriate cleaning materials.

Software Updates

Install operating system and application updates to improve performance and security.

Antivirus Scanning

Use trusted security software to check for malicious programs.

Storage Management

Remove unnecessary files and organize important documents.

Backup

Create copies of important information to prevent permanent data loss.

Temperature Management

Provide proper ventilation and avoid blocking cooling openings.

B. Corrective Maintenance

Corrective maintenance involves fixing problems after they occur.

Examples:

Replacing a damaged keyboard.

Repairing a faulty storage device.

Reinstalling corrupted software.

Replacing a defective cooling fan.

Fixing network connection problems.

C. Software Maintenance

Software maintenance focuses on keeping programs and operating systems functional and updated.

Examples:

Installing security patches.

Updating applications.

Removing unnecessary programs.

Fixing software errors.

Updating device drivers when necessary.

D. Hardware Maintenance

Hardware maintenance focuses on the physical condition of computer components.

Examples:

Cleaning external surfaces.

Checking cables and connections.

Inspecting cooling fans.

Ensuring proper ventilation.

Replacing defective components through qualified technicians.

E. Importance of Regular Maintenance

Regular maintenance can:

Improve computer reliability.

Reduce unexpected system failures.

Protect stored information.

Maintain system performance.

Reduce repair costs.

Extend equipment lifespan.

16. Data Backup, Recovery, and Cloud Storage

Data is one of the most valuable resources stored in a computer system.

Losing important files can affect students, businesses, organizations, and individuals.

Data backup and recovery are important practices that protect information against accidental deletion, hardware failure, malware, and other problems.

A. Data Backup

A backup is a separate copy of important information that can be used if the original files become unavailable.

Common backup methods include:

Full Backup

Copies all selected files and information.

Incremental Backup

Copies only the information that has changed since the most recent backup.

Differential Backup

Copies information that has changed since the last full backup.

B. Local Backup

Local backup stores copies of information on physical devices.

Examples:

External hard drives.

USB flash drives.

Network-attached storage devices.

C. Cloud Backup

Cloud backup stores copies of information on remote servers that can be accessed through the internet.

Examples:

Google Drive.

Microsoft OneDrive.

Apple iCloud.

Dropbox.

D. Data Recovery

Data recovery refers to methods used to restore lost, damaged, or inaccessible information.

Recovery may involve restoring backup files, using recovery software, or seeking professional assistance.

E. The 3-2-1 Backup Rule

The 3-2-1 backup rule is a commonly recommended data protection strategy.

It suggests maintaining:

Three copies of important data.

Two different types of storage media.

One copy stored in a separate location.

This approach helps reduce the risk of losing all copies because of one incident.

17. Virtualization and Virtual Machines

Virtualization is a technology that allows one physical computer to run multiple virtual computing environments.

A virtual machine (VM) is a software-based computer that behaves like a physical computer.

It has virtual hardware, an operating system, memory, storage, and applications.

A. How Virtualization Works

A physical computer provides the hardware resources needed to create virtual machines.

A software layer called a hypervisor manages the virtual machines and distributes the available resources.

Each virtual machine operates independently within its assigned environment.

B. Types of Hypervisors

Type 1 Hypervisor

Runs directly on the physical computer hardware.

It is commonly used in servers and enterprise environments.

Type 2 Hypervisor

Runs as an application on an existing operating system.

It is commonly used for learning, software testing, and personal experimentation.

C. Examples of Virtualization Software

Oracle VirtualBox.

VMware Workstation.

Microsoft Hyper-V.

VMware ESXi.

D. Advantages of Virtualization

Allows multiple operating systems on one physical computer.

Helps test software in separate environments.

Improves hardware resource utilization.

Reduces the need for additional physical computers.

Supports server management and development.

E. Applications of Virtualization

Virtualization is used in:

Software development.

IT education.

Server management.

Application testing.

Cloud computing.

Cybersecurity laboratories.

18. Ergonomics and Health in Computer Use

Computer ergonomics refers to designing and arranging computer equipment and workspaces to support comfort, safety, and efficient work.

Proper computer ergonomics can help reduce physical discomfort during extended computer use.

A. Proper Sitting Position

Users should maintain a comfortable sitting position when working with computers.

Recommended practices:

Keep the back supported.

Keep feet comfortably supported.

Avoid awkward wrist positions.

Position the screen at a comfortable viewing height.

Keep the keyboard and mouse within easy reach.

B. Proper Monitor Placement

The monitor should be positioned at a comfortable distance and height.

Users should avoid excessive glare and adjust screen brightness according to the surrounding environment.

C. Keyboard and Mouse Position

The keyboard and mouse should be positioned to allow relaxed shoulders and comfortable arm movement.

Users should avoid excessive force when typing or clicking.

D. Taking Breaks

Regular breaks help reduce eye strain and physical discomfort.

Users can briefly look away from the screen, stand, stretch, and change positions.

E. Proper Lighting

Workspaces should have adequate lighting to reduce glare and improve visibility.

F. Importance of Ergonomics

Proper ergonomics can:

Improve working comfort.

Reduce unnecessary physical strain.

Support good posture.

Help maintain productivity.

Encourage healthy computer habits.

19. Selecting the Right Computer Hardware and Software

Choosing computer hardware and software depends on the user's needs, budget, and intended activities.

Different users require different computer specifications.

A student who mainly creates documents may not need the same hardware as a professional video editor or a computer programmer.

A. Identifying User Requirements

Before purchasing a computer, users should identify the activities they plan to perform.

Examples:

Basic School Activities

Recommended considerations:

Reliable processor.

Sufficient RAM.

SSD storage.

Comfortable keyboard.

Suitable display.

Programming

Recommended considerations:

Multicore processor.

Adequate RAM.

SSD storage.

Compatible operating system.

Development software.

Graphic Design and Video Editing

Recommended considerations:

Powerful CPU.

Dedicated or capable integrated GPU.

Sufficient RAM.

Fast storage.

High-quality display.

Gaming

Recommended considerations:

Capable CPU.

Dedicated GPU.

Adequate RAM.

Sufficient storage.

Monitor with suitable refresh rate.

B. Important Factors When Choosing Hardware

Performance

Consider the processor, memory, and graphics capabilities.

Storage

Choose sufficient storage capacity for documents, applications, and multimedia files.

Compatibility

Make sure the components and software can work together.

Portability

Consider whether a desktop, laptop, or tablet is more appropriate.

Budget

Choose equipment that meets the user's needs without unnecessary expenses.

Upgradeability

Consider whether RAM, storage, or other components can be upgraded in the future.

C. Choosing Software

Users should also consider software requirements.

Important factors include:

Compatibility with the operating system.

Required features.

Security and reliability.

Licensing conditions.

Ease of use.

Cost and available support.

Making informed decisions helps users select appropriate computer systems for their activities.

20. The Future of Computer Hardware and Software

Computer technology continues to develop through improvements in electronic components, software engineering, and communication systems.

Future computer systems are expected to become more efficient, intelligent, connected, and specialized.

A. Artificial Intelligence in Computing

Artificial intelligence is becoming increasingly integrated into computer hardware and software.

AI-powered systems can assist with information processing, image recognition, language translation, and decision support.

B. Advanced Processors

Processor manufacturers continue developing chips with improved performance and energy efficiency.

New processor designs may include specialized processing units for artificial intelligence, graphics, and other computing tasks.

C. Edge Computing

Edge computing processes information closer to where data is generated instead of sending everything to distant cloud servers.

It can help reduce delays and support applications that require quick responses.

Examples include smart cameras, industrial sensors, and connected vehicles.

D. Green Computing

Green computing focuses on designing, using, and disposing of computer equipment in environmentally responsible ways.

It includes:

Reducing energy consumption.

Improving hardware efficiency.

Recycling electronic waste.

Extending device lifespan.

Developing environmentally friendly technologies.

E. Wearable Computing

Wearable computing involves small electronic devices that can be worn on the body.

Examples:

Smartwatches.

Fitness trackers.

Smart glasses.

Health-monitoring devices.

F. Neuromorphic Computing

Neuromorphic computing is an emerging field that designs computer systems inspired by the structure and operation of biological nervous systems.

It aims to develop specialized computing architectures that may perform certain tasks efficiently.

G. Advanced Robotics

Modern robots increasingly combine sensors, processors, software, and artificial intelligence.

They are used in manufacturing, research, healthcare, agriculture, and exploration.

H. More Secure Computing Systems

Future software and hardware will continue to develop security features to protect digital information and connected devices.

Security will remain an important part of computer system design.

21. Ethical and Responsible Use of Computer Technology

Computers provide powerful tools for communication, education, and information sharing. However, users must understand their responsibilities when using technology.

Computer ethics refers to moral principles that guide the responsible use of computers and digital information.

A. Respecting Privacy

Users should avoid accessing, sharing, or collecting another person's private information without permission.

B. Respecting Copyright

Copyright protects the original work of creators.

Users should avoid copying or distributing protected software, documents, images, and other digital content without proper permission.

C. Avoiding Plagiarism

Plagiarism occurs when someone presents another person's work or ideas as their own without proper acknowledgment.

Students should cite sources when using information from books, websites, articles, and other materials.

D. Responsible Online Communication

Users should communicate respectfully and avoid cyberbullying, harassment, and the spread of false information.

E. Protecting Digital Identity

Users should carefully manage personal information and avoid sharing sensitive details with unknown individuals or untrusted websites.

F. Proper Use of Artificial Intelligence

AI tools should be used responsibly.

Users should verify information, respect intellectual property, protect personal data, and follow their school's or organization's policies.

Importance of Computer Ethics

Computer ethics encourages users to:

Respect other people's rights.

Protect personal information.

Use technology honestly.

Avoid harmful online behavior.

Follow laws and software licenses.

Become responsible digital citizens.

22. Practical Activities: Understanding Hardware and Software

Practical activities help students understand the relationship between computer hardware and software.

The following activities can be performed in a computer laboratory or through supervised demonstrations.

Activity 1: Identifying Computer Hardware

Objective: Identify the different hardware components of a computer system.

Instructions:

Observe a desktop computer or laptop.

Identify its external hardware components.

Identify the internal components through diagrams or supervised demonstrations.

Classify each component according to its function.

Examples:

HardwareClassification
KeyboardInput
MouseInput
MonitorOutput
PrinterOutput
SSDStorage
CPUProcessing
RouterCommunication

Activity 2: Identifying Computer Software

Objective: Understand the different categories of computer software.

Instructions:

Observe the programs installed on a computer.

Identify the operating system.

Identify application software.

Identify utility software.

Classify each program according to its purpose.

Examples:

SoftwareClassification
WindowsOperating System
Microsoft WordApplication Software
Google ChromeApplication Software
AntivirusUtility Software
Device DriverSystem Software
Visual Studio CodeProgramming Tool

Activity 3: Understanding the IPOS Cycle

Objective: Understand how a computer processes information.

Instructions:

Open a calculator application.

Enter two numbers.

Allow the computer to calculate the result.

Observe the displayed answer.

Save the result if necessary.

Identify the following:

Input: Numbers entered.

Process: Mathematical calculation.

Output: Displayed answer.

Storage: Saved information.

Activity 4: File Management

Objective: Practice organizing digital files.

Instructions:

Create a new folder.

Give the folder an appropriate name.

Create or save a document inside it.

Rename the document.

Move the document to another folder.

Identify its file extension.

This activity teaches students how to organize and manage digital information.

23. Important Differences Between Hardware and Software

Hardware and software are two essential parts of a computer system, but they have different characteristics.

HardwareSoftware
Physical componentsPrograms and instructions
Can be touchedCannot be physically touched
Manufactured or assembledDeveloped or programmed
Can experience physical damageCan experience errors or corruption
Requires software for useful operationRequires hardware to execute
Examples: CPU, RAM, monitorExamples: Windows, Word, Chrome

Important Differences Between RAM and ROM

RAMROM
Random Access MemoryRead Only Memory
Usually volatileNon-volatile
Temporarily stores active dataStores persistent instructions
Supports running applicationsSupports firmware-related functions
Contents normally disappear when power is removedContents remain without power

Important Differences Between HDD and SSD

HDDSSD
Uses magnetic storageUses flash memory
Contains moving partsHas no moving mechanical parts
Usually slowerUsually faster
Often cheaper per gigabyteOften more expensive per gigabyte
Sensitive to physical shockGenerally more resistant to physical shock

Important Differences Between System Software and Application Software

System SoftwareApplication Software
Manages computer operationsPerforms specific user tasks
Helps hardware and applications workHelps users complete activities
Runs as part of the system environmentRuns with the support of system software
Examples: Windows, LinuxExamples: Word, Excel, Chrome

24. Additional Important Computer Terminologies

Peripheral – An external hardware device connected to a computer.

Motherboard – The main circuit board that connects computer components.

CPU – The Central Processing Unit responsible for executing instructions.

GPU – The Graphics Processing Unit responsible for graphics and parallel processing tasks.

PSU – The Power Supply Unit that provides converted electrical power to computer components.

BIOS – Basic Input/Output System, a type of firmware used for hardware initialization and startup functions.

UEFI – Unified Extensible Firmware Interface, a modern firmware interface used by many computers.

Firmware – Software stored in a hardware device that controls its basic operations.

Driver – Software that allows an operating system to communicate with a hardware device.

Cache – High-speed memory that stores frequently accessed information.

Pixel – The smallest individual element of a digital image.

Resolution – The number of pixels used to display an image.

Refresh Rate – The number of times a display updates its image per second.

Bandwidth – The maximum data transfer capacity of a communication connection.

Latency – The time delay between an action and its corresponding response.

LAN – Local Area Network.

WAN – Wide Area Network.

PAN – Personal Area Network.

MAN – Metropolitan Area Network.

USB – Universal Serial Bus.

HDMI – High-Definition Multimedia Interface.

SSD – Solid-State Drive.

HDD – Hard Disk Drive.

OCR – Optical Character Recognition.

OMR – Optical Mark Recognition.

MICR – Magnetic Ink Character Recognition.

NIC – Network Interface Card.

IDE – Integrated Development Environment.

SDLC – Software Development Life Cycle.

VM – Virtual Machine.

Hypervisor – Software that creates and manages virtual machines.

Malware – Malicious software designed to harm or compromise computer systems.

Firewall – A security system that monitors and controls network traffic.

Encryption – The process of converting information into a protected format.

Backup – A separate copy of information used for recovery.

Cloud Storage – Online storage that allows users to access files through the internet.

Virtual Memory – A memory management technique that uses storage to extend available memory.

Open-Source Software – Software distributed under a license that permits access to its source code and specified forms of use or modification.

Proprietary Software – Software controlled by an owner under specific license conditions.

Troubleshooting – The process of identifying and solving computer problems.
